title: "Overview of Ecosystem Service: Pest Control"
format:

    embed-resources: true
    standalone: true

Biological pest control is valued as the share of the organic harvest owed to natural enemies, at
the organic producer price. The base year is 2019.

The scope is organic agriculture only, by design: the underlying evidence measures the yield
effect of predators where synthetic pesticides are absent, and no comparable estimate exists
for conventional systems. The full value is attributed to nature, with no human-input share
taken out (λ = 1), unlike the neighbouring crop rows.

## Source

The write-up is `Pest_Control.docx` (3 November 2026), with
`pest_control_additionaldocumentation.docx` (4 November 2026), in the shared folder of current
write-ups. The code follows the organic cleaning, the valuation and the Monte Carlo of
`wsidemoholm/value_org` at fb40d8c. On the service owner's advice, conventional yields and prices
come from the FAOSTAT tables of the ported `crop_benefits` chain, which crop provision also values,
in place of that repository's price imputation.

## Quantity

Organic production per crop and country is the organic area, times the country's conventional
FAOSTAT yield, times an organic-to-conventional yield ratio per FAO crop group.

The yield ratios are the service owner's group models, run on the exact file its code downloads: Ponisio et al.
(2015), doi:10.5061/dryad.hf305, `DataForSubmitting.csv`, MD5 3bd682813cea2be9a5acba17ce35cc30, taken from its Zenodo
copy, record 5002287. All 15 numbers in Table 1 of the additional documentation and the 3 for cereals in the August
appendix match at their printed precision. The owner's own `yield_ratios_FAO.csv` is not held, so agreement at full
precision is not shown.

The organic area is FiBL's extract, cleaned as the service owner does:

- FiBL's country and crop names go to FAOSTAT's. FiBL crops under one FAOSTAT item are summed.
- A country without a FAOSTAT crop series and a crop without a FAOSTAT counterpart are removed.
- A FAOSTAT aggregate, such as unspecified fruit, is left unvalued, because no yield or price
  belongs to it.
- A negative area becomes zero. A cell holding two numbers as text gives its first number, which
  matters in 2019 only for rye in Austria and Ukraine.
- A record above ten times its neighbouring years and also above the crop's whole harvested area
  takes the mean of those years.
- France's nut area of 2008-2020, which FiBL reports mostly as one aggregate, is split into walnuts,
  chestnuts, hazelnuts, almonds, pistachios and other nuts by Agence Bio's mainland shares of the same
  year, so each year's total is kept. A regional cell Agence Bio withholds for confidentiality (`NC`)
  adds no area to a share: its area is unknown, not zero. In 2019 the 15,147 hectares split into
  8,168 of walnuts, 5,652 of chestnuts, 631 of almonds, 563 of hazelnuts and 133 of other nuts, the
  last without a FAOSTAT yield or price, so that row stays missing. 9 of the 52 mainland nut cells of
  2019 are withheld.

In 2019 FiBL reports 11,931,709 hectares. Of these, 703 are in countries without a FAOSTAT series,
702,518 in crops without a counterpart and 1,083,104 in aggregates. One record is corrected:
walnuts in Kyrgyzstan, from 3,199 to 175 hectares. Across all years the same rule corrects seven
records, the number the additional documentation gives.

## Price

The organic producer price is the conventional price times an organic-to-conventional price ratio.
The conventional price is the shared table's 2019 USD price, resolved at the country, or else its
subregion, its region or the world. The price ratio is the one matched for that crop, country and
year in the USDA trade data, or else the mean of its FAO group.

Both read only the ratios within a plausibility limit, `pest_control_organic_premium_plausibility_times`,
set to the service owner's 10. A trade unit value can compare an organic and a conventional product that
differ in processing, packaging or quality, so a ratio above 10 or below 1/10 is left out before the group
means are taken, and its crop, country and year take the group mean. The limits themselves are kept. The
limit leaves out 15 of the 2,459 ratios, 10 above and 5 below, and the task writes them to
`pest_control_price_ratios_left_out.csv`. Twelve are stimulant crops, mostly tea, and they lower that
group's mean from 1.633 to 1.420. One reaches a 2019 value: Viet Nam's tea, whose matched ratio of 38.01
is left out, so the row takes that group mean of 1.420.

## Valuation

Per crop $i$, country $j$:

$$
\text{Value}_{ij} = \left(1 - e^{-\text{lnRR}_{g(i)}}\right) \; A_{ij} \; y_{ij} \, r_{g(i)} \; p_{ij} \, \pi_{ij}
$$

where $\text{lnRR}_{g(i)}$ is the crop group's meta-analytic log response ratio, $A$ the organic
area, $y$ the conventional yield, $r$ the yield ratio, $p$ the conventional price and $\pi$ the
price ratio. The first factor is the fraction of the observed yield that disappears without natural
enemies. The vegetable effect applies to vegetables, oilseeds and pulses, and the other-crops effect
to fruit, nuts and stimulants. Cereals are not valued, because their effect does not differ
significantly from zero (`pest_control_include_cereals`). Roots and tubers, sugar crops and forage
carry no benefit. A crop in a group outside these lists is unclassified and stays missing.

## Uncertainty

The published value is the mean of 10,000 Monte Carlo simulations, with the 2.5th and 97.5th
percentiles beside it. Each simulation draws:

- one lnRR per effect category from a normal distribution, used for every crop in that category
- one yield ratio per FAO group from a log-normal distribution
- one price ratio per FAO group from a log-normal distribution, for crops without a matched ratio

Draws are shared across countries so errors do not cancel when values are summed. Areas, yields,
conventional prices and matched price ratios stay fixed.

**The interval leaves out conventional price uncertainty, and its size is not measured.** The service
owner also draws each imputed price from its prediction interval, and the shared FAOSTAT table has no
such spread. In the central value, 93.3% sits on a country's own price and 6.7% on a price resolved at
the subregion, region or world, held fixed.

The table also carries the central value, every parameter at its point estimate. It exceeds the
mean mainly because the benefit's expected value is below its value at the mean lnRR. The world uncertainty
table holds the exact expectation of the draws as a check on their mean.

By exact calculation, the other-crops benefit carries 95.6% of the modeled parameter variance of the world
value, the vegetable benefit 2.9%, the yield ratios 1.2% and the group-mean price ratios under 0.1%. These
shares assume independent draws across parameter families and hold matched price ratios, conventional prices,
yields and areas fixed. They are not shares of all scientific uncertainty, because model choice, transfer,
coverage and the omitted price draws sit outside them. They were measured on the first run of this code, at the
rounded yield ratios and before the shared price filters, and are not re-measured.

## Coverage

The figures below are from the isolated run at the exact yield ratios on the filtered shared prices, which is not yet
the published table.

The table is one row for each of the account's 250 countries, base year 2019, in 2019 USD. Of the
250, 124 carry a value, totalling \$5,195,473,666.75, with a 95% interval for the world of
\$1,389,762,095.71 to \$8,402,623,749.17, 9 are zeros and 117 are missing. That total is the Monte Carlo
mean. The exact expectation of the same draws is \$5,181,246,896.82.

A total covers only the crops with data, so `pest_control_coverage` says what each number means, and
no missing contribution is estimated:

| Coverage | Countries | Value | Meaning |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `complete_value` | 80 | \$4,033,690,572.87 | a total, and every crop with a benefit in its crop table has inputs |
| `partial_value` | 44 | \$1,161,783,093.88 | a total, beside 110 crops with a benefit that lack an input |
| `complete_zero` | 9 | \$0 | only crops without a benefit in its crop table, a zero by the write-up's rule |
| `zero_with_missing` | 1 | missing | Paraguay: its computed crops are zero, but one crop with a benefit lacks an input, so the zero is not known |
| `missing_inputs` | 3 | missing | Gambia, Guinea and Mauritius: organic crops, none with inputs |
| `left_out_area_only` | 15 | missing | organic area only in aggregates or crops without a FAOSTAT counterpart |
| `no_organic_area` | 98 | missing | FiBL reports no organic area in 2019 |

The 118 crops with a benefit that lack an input hold 68,005 hectares against 4,754,739 valued, so
98.6% of the crop table's area with a benefit is valued. A crop without a benefit contributes
nothing with or without its inputs, so it does not count as missing. "Complete" refers to the crop
table only. Another 1,801,472 hectares never reach it (15.1% of FiBL's area), including 1,158,621 in
`complete_value` countries, and `pest_control_area_left_out_ha` holds them per country.

The 9 zeros follow the write-up's rule and are not measured. Seven hold cereals, which the write-up
leaves out because their effect does not differ significantly from zero, and turn positive when
`pest_control_include_cereals` is on. Mali and Tajikistan hold only seed cotton, in a group absent from
the effect-size studies.

The service owner's code keeps a country only when its mean is above zero, so the 9 zeros read as missing
in that table. Paraguay reads missing on both sides, for different reasons. The service owner's published
simulations hold only its sugar cane and wheat, both without a benefit, so its mean is zero and the filter
removes it. The library's crop table also holds 47.3 hectares of other oil seeds, which carry a benefit and
have no FAOSTAT yield or price, so the coverage rule makes its total missing. That rule is how the library
treats a missing input, and it shows no error in the service owner's code. The other missing countries are
missing in both. These statements rest on the code and the published simulations, because the current table
is not held.

## Inputs

All paths and parameters come from `es_parameters.csv` under the `pest_control` service key,
each with a source row beside it: the FiBL extract, the United Kingdom statistics, Agence Bio's regional
areas with their sha256 and the years they split, the FAO classification, the matched price ratios, the shared FAOSTAT tables, the 2019 FAOSTAT slice for
crop items and harvested area, the effect sizes and yield ratios with their standard errors, and
the number of draws and the seed.

## Output

`gep_calculation` writes `gep_by_country_base_year.csv` into its own task directory, holding the
r250 identifiers and attributes, `year`, `pest_control_gep`, `pest_control_gep_lower`,
`pest_control_gep_upper`, `pest_control_gep_central`, `pest_control_gep_reference`,
`pest_control_coverage`, the counts `pest_control_crops`, `pest_control_crops_valued`,
`pest_control_crops_no_benefit` and `pest_control_crops_missing`, and the hectares
`pest_control_area_valued_ha`, `pest_control_area_no_benefit_ha`, `pest_control_area_missing_ha` and
`pest_control_area_left_out_ha`. Beside it, `pest_control_by_crop_country.csv` holds the per-crop rows
with the note naming any missing factor, `pest_control_world_uncertainty.csv` the world statistics,
`pest_control_coverage_summary.csv` the same counts for the world with the value by coverage,
`pest_control_organic_area_spikes.csv` the corrected records, `pest_control_price_ratios_left_out.csv`
the price ratios outside the plausibility limit and `pest_control_france_nut_shares.csv` the Agence Bio
shares with their count of withheld cells.

## Reference

The reference column applies the service owner's current summary to the owner's published
simulations (Zenodo record 17993071, December 2025). Those simulations are older than fb40d8c: they
use other yield ratios and other prices, and draw ratios per row, so their means compare and their
intervals do not. The reference totals \$5,386,426,093.48 over the same 124 countries. This is a
comparison with the published simulations, not a reproduction of fb40d8c.

## What the value rests on

The interval draws parameters and holds the choices below fixed. These are sizes of those choices, not
estimates, and none changes the code. They were measured on the first run of this code, at the rounded yield ratios,
before the shared price filters, the price-ratio plausibility limit and the French nut split, and are not re-measured. Percentages are of that run's exact expectation,
\$5,190,393,846.19, except the shares of the central value.

- The benefit's evidence. Boldorini et al. (2024) hold 47 yield comparisons from 19 studies. The other-crops
  effect comes from 9 of them, in 7 studies of apples, cocoa and coffee, and carries 85.4% of the central
  value. Crops named in those yield experiments hold 20.6% of it. Grapes, tea and olives hold 46.9% and
  have no yield experiment.
- One study. Dropping one of the 19 from a refit of their public data moves the expectation between -13.4%
  (a cocoa study in Indonesia) and +18.5% (a coffee study in Brazil).
- The model. Boldorini et al. report no detectable yield effect once crop phylogeny is accounted for, on
  13 species, and urge caution. At those estimates the expectation falls 33.0% and the interval crosses
  zero. Their climate moderators on yield are not significant, on 47 comparisons, which a refit of their model
  repeats (p = 0.36). A test without a significant difference does not show that the effect transfers.
- The yield ratios. The stimulant ratio is 7 coffee comparisons in 3 studies, and tea takes it with no
  comparison of its own. The write-up's comparison, de la Cruz et al. (2023), moves the expectation +5.6%
  in total: +11.1% for fruit and nuts alone, -5.7% for stimulants alone. Dropping one study moves it at most
  1.7%. By continent, oilseeds differ (p < 0.001, with 109 of 119 rows in North America). Fruit and nuts,
  vegetables and pulses show no significant difference at the 5% level, which does not show that they transfer,
  since Latin America, Africa and Oceania hold 1.1%, 1.1% and 0.6% of the rows. Stimulants sit on one continent,
  so they cannot be tested.
- Where the evidence sits. Asia holds 39.4% of the central value and 12.1% of the yield-ratio rows. North
  America holds 12.5% of the value and 45.0% of the rows.
- The price ratios. The write-up's comparison, Crowder and Reganold (2015), moves the expectation +18.3% on
  rows without a matched ratio. The group mean on every row moves it -5.3%.

## What is open

- The owner's current table. `pest_control_2019.csv` from a run of fb40d8c is not held. It cannot be rebuilt
  from what is held, because that run also reads the FAOSTAT release and the IMF exchange-rate export it was
  made with.
- Prices above the country. Coffee in Uganda and Tanzania takes the shared table's subregion price of
  \$844.50 per tonne, against about \$2,900 in the published simulations.
- Two-number cells. A cell's second number has no label, and the first number is kept.
